<article class="proj" id="wire-bonding" data-date="2026-10">
<div class="meta"><p class="date">October 2026 · Coursework</p>
<ul class="tags"><li>FEA</li><li>Abaqus</li><li>Semiconductor packaging</li><li>Communication</li></ul></div>
<div class="body"><h3>Finite element analysis of the wire bonding process</h3>
<span class="stat">821 MPa peak stress at 25 µm compression</span>
<p><b>Problem.</b> Wire bonding involves complex interactions between the wire, bond tool, and substrate. These can cause deformation and residual stresses that affect the reliability of the finished assembly, and simulation can flag issues before manufacturing.</p>
<p><b>Approach.</b> I built an implicit Abaqus model from the provided materials and geometry. I modified the geometry to improve accuracy, modeled half of the system with symmetry to reduce element count, defined the interactions between components, and set boundary conditions for the capillary and bulk die.</p>
<p><b>Result.</b> The simulation showed a peak stress of 821 MPa after the capillary compressed the softened wire by 25 µm. The project strengthened my finite element modeling experience.</p><div class="figs ultra">
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="1000" height="425" alt="Initial state of the wire bonding model (mirrored): silicon die, bonding pad, softened wire, and capillary." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Initial state of the wire bonding model (mirrored): silicon die, bonding pad, softened wire, and capillary.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="1000" height="425" alt="Final state (mirrored): the capillary has moved down 25 µm, compressing the softened wire." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Final state (mirrored): the capillary has moved down 25 µm, compressing the softened wire.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
</div>
</article>

<article class="proj" id="mri" data-date="2026-08">
<div class="meta"><p class="date">August 2026</p>
<ul class="tags"><li>Signal processing</li><li>Numerical methods</li><li>C++</li><li>MATLAB</li><li>OpenCV</li><li>MS Excel</li><li>Communication</li></ul>
<p style="margin-top:12px;font:600 15px var(--sans)"><a href="https://github.com/UnderscoreLogs" rel="noopener">Source on GitHub</a></p></div>
<div class="body"><h3>MRI k-space acquisition simulator</h3>
<span class="stat">6 trajectories compared at equal sampling</span><span class="stat">NUFFT up to ~4× faster at comparable PSNR/SSIM</span>
<p><b>Problem.</b> MRI scanners acquire frequency-domain k-space data rather than a direct image. Shorter scans need less k-space data, but that can introduce artifacts and reduce image detail.</p>
<p><b>Approach.</b> I visualized k-space data and reconstructed a fully sampled reference image. I then removed selected phase-encoding lines to simulate undersampling, applied the same inverse FFT reconstruction, and compared sharpness, contrast, and aliasing across Cartesian, random, radial, spiral, VDC, and VDR trajectories. Test images included Lena, Barbara, Cameraman, Shepp-Logan, two real brain MRIs from OpenNeuro, and a real knee MRI from the NYU fastMRI dataset.</p>
<p><b>Result.</b> Fully sampled k-space gave the clearest image. Keeping central k-space preserved overall anatomy and contrast, while dropping high-frequency data reduced edge detail. Uniform undersampling shortened acquisition but caused visible aliasing. I also tested robustness to simulated motion and noise, and documented the methods, results, and limitations in a 19-page research paper.</p><div class="figs">
<figure class="wide"><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="1000" height="627" alt="Sampling locations of the six k-space trajectories, each shown at the same sampling percentage." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Sampling locations of the six k-space trajectories, each shown at the same sampling percentage.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="wide"><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="1200" height="1442" alt="Reconstructions from each trajectory at 50% sampling, with PSNR and SSIM for each. Test images: Lena, Cameraman, Barbara, Shepp-Logan, two brain MRIs from OpenNeuro, and a knee MRI from the NYU fastMRI dataset." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Reconstructions from each trajectory at 50% sampling, with PSNR and SSIM for each. Test images: Lena, Cameraman, Barbara, Shepp-Logan, two brain MRIs from OpenNeuro, and a knee MRI from the NYU fastMRI dataset.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
</div>
</article>

<article class="proj" id="heatsink" data-date="2026-07">
<div class="meta"><p class="date">July 2026 · Research team</p>
<ul class="tags"><li>Thermal management</li><li>Semiconductor packaging</li><li>FEA</li><li>ANSYS</li><li>CAD</li><li>Fusion 360</li><li>Additive manufacturing</li><li>Teamwork</li><li>Communication</li></ul></div>
<div class="body"><h3>Thermally conductive polymer heatsink</h3>
<span class="stat">43.7% lower simulated peak temperature</span><span class="stat">~100 °C vs. 140 °C+ steady state</span>
<p><b>Problem.</b> Heatsinks reduce thermal resistance and improve heat dissipation. Machining limits design freedom, while additive manufacturing allows complex, optimized geometries.</p>
<p><b>Approach.</b> I worked with three other undergraduate researchers in the team of Dr. Chris Bailey, former IEEE Electronics Packaging Society President. I oversaw manufacturing: researching the material (TC-Poly Ice9), modeling the heatsink in Fusion 360, and programming the 3D printer. I also simulated thermal performance in ANSYS, evaluated prints with a thermal test vehicle and thermal imaging, and presented weekly updates.</p>
<p><b>Result.</b> Simulation showed a 43.7% reduction in peak temperature versus conventional TPU, with better temperature uniformity. In natural-convection testing, the TC-Poly heatsink reached about 100 °C steady state, compared with more than 140 °C for TPU. TC-Poly shows strong potential for unconventional heatsink designs.</p><div class="figs three">
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="503" height="302" alt="Simulated maximum temperature by heatsink material." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Simulated maximum temperature by heatsink material.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="473" height="277" alt="ANSYS thermal simulation of the TC-Poly heatsink." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>ANSYS thermal simulation of the TC-Poly heatsink.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="330" height="441" alt="Thermal image of the conventional TPU heatsink during testing." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Thermal image of the conventional TPU heatsink during testing.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
</div>
</article>

<article class="proj" id="ai-module" data-date="2026-07">
<div class="meta"><p class="date">July 2026 · Intel/ASU REU</p>
<ul class="tags"><li>Semiconductor packaging</li><li>Teamwork</li><li>Communication</li></ul></div>
<div class="body"><h3>Heterogeneous integrated AI accelerator module</h3>
<span class="stat">Led the Intel research track</span>
<p><b>Goal.</b> Design a heterogeneous integrated AI accelerator module by comparing Intel and Amkor advanced packaging technologies.</p>
<p><b>Approach.</b> I worked with four undergraduate researchers from chemical, mechanical, optical, and electrical engineering. We defined what an AI accelerator package must deliver (interconnect density, HBM integration, power delivery, thermal and mechanical integrity, scalability) and used those criteria to compare the two companies. I led the Intel research on EMIB, Foveros 3D, Foveros Direct, and combined 3.5D integration, using Intel documentation and Dr. Ravi Mahajan’s REU lectures. I also helped create the overview figures and coordinated with teammates on Amkor.</p>
<p><b>Result.</b> Both companies use embedded silicon for higher interconnect density, with Intel’s EMIB and Amkor’s S-Connect the strongest options for AI accelerators. We concluded Intel’s EMIB and Foveros currently offer the most capable high-performance platform, while Amkor’s cost-focused approach shows how advanced packaging is shaping the future of AI performance. We presented the findings at the program’s final review.</p><div class="figs">
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="970" height="646" alt="Final design presentation: Intel vs. Amkor heterogeneous integrated AI accelerator module." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Final design presentation: Intel vs. Amkor heterogeneous integrated AI accelerator module.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="634" height="478" alt="Receiving the REU certificate at the Intel Summer REU on Semiconductor Packaging program review." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Receiving the REU certificate at the Intel Summer REU on Semiconductor Packaging program review.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
</div>
</article>

<article class="proj" id="fourier" data-date="2026-07">
<div class="meta"><p class="date">July 2026</p>
<ul class="tags"><li>Signal processing</li><li>Numerical methods</li><li>PDE simulation</li><li>C++</li><li>MATLAB</li><li>MS Excel</li><li>Communication</li></ul>
<p style="margin-top:12px;font:600 15px var(--sans)"><a href="https://github.com/UnderscoreLogs" rel="noopener">Source on GitHub</a></p></div>
<div class="body"><h3>Fourier transform project collection</h3>
<span class="stat">15 projects</span><span class="stat">47-page technical paper</span>
<p><b>Goal.</b> Learn and apply Fourier methods to signal and image processing, simulate physical systems, and reconstruct MRI scans from k-space data.</p>
<p><b>Approach.</b> I implemented algorithms in C++ and MATLAB across four areas: FFT/STFT denoising with frequency-domain filtering, PDE simulation of heat and wave behavior, image processing with Fourier and STFT methods, and MRI reconstruction from real and simulated k-space data.</p>
<p><b>Result.</b> The collection shows how Fourier methods support analysis, simulation, and reconstruction, and exposes tradeoffs such as detail loss from filtering and artifacts from STFT windowing.</p><div class="figs">
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="440" height="264" alt="Denoising a noisy signal with a short-time Fourier transform." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Denoising a noisy signal with a short-time Fourier transform.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="440" height="265" alt="Denoising the same signal with a regular FFT." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Denoising the same signal with a regular FFT.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="440" height="293" alt="Power spectrum density of a noisy chirp signal." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Power spectrum density of a noisy chirp signal.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="440" height="289" alt="Custom STFT spectrogram of the same chirp." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Custom STFT spectrogram of the same chirp.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="440" height="261" alt="Waterfall plot of a PDE simulation of a 1D Gaussian wave." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Waterfall plot of a PDE simulation of a 1D Gaussian wave.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="427" height="262" alt="PDE simulation of the damped wave equation for a 2D negative Gaussian pulse." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>PDE simulation of the damped wave equation for a 2D negative Gaussian pulse.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="440" height="329" alt="Original image." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Original image.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="440" height="340" alt="Image denoised with a custom 2D STFT." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Image denoised with a custom 2D STFT.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
</div>
</article>

<article class="proj wip" id="carabiner" style="padding-left:20px" data-date="2026-10">
<div class="meta"><p class="date">Present · CAD class final project</p>
<ul class="tags"><li>CAD</li><li>SolidWorks</li><li>FEA</li><li>Technical drawing</li><li>Reverse engineering</li><li>Engineering design</li></ul></div>
<div class="body"><h3>Carabiner reverse engineering</h3>
<span class="stat">Frame complete, mechanism underway</span>
<p><b>Goal.</b> Reverse engineer a carabiner from scratch in SolidWorks, then run an FEA to evaluate its structural capability.</p>
<p><b>Approach.</b> I photographed the carabiner on grid paper, imported the image as a scaled sketch picture, traced the profile with splines and arcs, and refined it until the model matched the physical part. The frame is built as a solid body and matches the measured geometry.</p>
<p><b>Next.</b> I’m designing the hinge and latching mechanism, then a fully mated assembly. Planned deliverables are a technical drawing next to a photo of the real part, and a SolidWorks Simulation study of how the carabiner responds to loading.</p><div class="figs">
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="1000" height="521" alt="Final SolidWorks model of the carabiner frame." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Final SolidWorks model of the carabiner frame.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="638" height="468" alt="Reference photo on grid paper used to reconstruct the frame profile." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>Reference photo on grid paper used to reconstruct the frame profile.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="479" height="634" alt="The original carabiner, disassembled." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>The original carabiner, disassembled.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="431" height="571" alt="The original carabiner, assembled." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>The original carabiner, assembled.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
</div>
</article>

<article class="proj" id="knife" data-date="2025-05">
<div class="meta"><p class="date">May 2025</p>
<ul class="tags"><li>Engineering design</li><li>CAD</li><li>Prototyping</li><li>Additive manufacturing</li><li>Forging</li><li>Heat treating</li></ul></div>
<div class="body"><h3>Knife design and fabrication</h3>
<span class="stat">2 knives, 2 design iterations</span>
<p><b>Problem.</b> A functional knife needs more than a good blade shape: handle ergonomics and heat treatment both affect comfort and performance. My first version showed handle discomfort and blade warping.</p>
<p><b>Approach.</b> I designed the knives in CAD, prototyped them with 3D printing, then sourced materials and made the blades. I built a propane forge from carved firebrick, heated 1084 steel to about 1,500 °F, quenched it in canola oil, and tempered each blade in a 400 °F oven for two three-hour cycles, aiming for about 60 HRC. Handles are G10 attached with epoxy and brass pins.</p>
<p><b>Problem solving.</b> The first blade warped in the quench. I traced it to uneven cooling: I had entered the oil at an angle and moved the blade side to side. For the second knife I quenched vertically with straight up-and-down motion, which cooled more evenly and addressed the warping. I also refined the handle ergonomics and tempering for V2.</p>
<p><b>Result.</b> Two finished knives, with the first version’s failures guiding the second. The project gave me hands-on experience with CAD, prototyping, material selection, forging, heat treatment, and iterative design.</p><div class="figs four">
<figure class=""><button class="frame" type="button" aria-label="Enlarge image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," width="361" height="480" alt="3D-printed prototype of version 1." loading="lazy"></button><figcaption>3D-printed prototype of version 1.</figcaption></figure>

(function(){var d=document.getElementById("lb");if(!d||!d.showModal)return;var im=d.querySelector("img"),c=d.querySelector("p");
document.querySelectorAll(".figs figure").forEach(function(f){var b=f.querySelector(".frame"),s=f.querySelector("img");
b.setAttribute("aria-label","Enlarge: "+f.querySelector("figcaption").textContent);
b.addEventListener("click",function(){im.src=s.src;im.alt=s.alt;c.textContent=f.querySelector("figcaption").textContent;d.showModal();});});

<script>
(function(){
var arts=[].slice.call(document.querySelectorAll("article.proj"));if(!arts.length)return;
var parent=arts[0].parentNode,anchor=arts[arts.length-1].nextElementSibling;
var sortSel=document.getElementById("sort"),skillSel=document.getElementById("skill"),count=document.getElementById("count");
var counts={};
arts.forEach(function(a,i){a.dataset.i=i;
 a._tags=[].slice.call(a.querySelectorAll(".meta .tags li")).map(function(li){return li.textContent.trim()});
 a._tags.forEach(function(t){counts[t]=(counts[t]||0)+1})});
Object.keys(counts).sort(function(x,y){return x.toLowerCase()<y.toLowerCase()?-1:1}).forEach(function(t){
 var o=document.createElement("option");o.value=t;o.textContent=t+" ("+counts[t]+")";skillSel.appendChild(o)});
function apply(){
 var order=sortSel.value,skill=skillSel.value,shown=0;
 arts.slice().sort(function(a,b){var x=a.dataset.date,y=b.dataset.date;if(x===y)return a.dataset.i-b.dataset.i;return order==="new"?(x<y?1:-1):(x<y?-1:1)})
 .forEach(function(a){
  parent.insertBefore(a,anchor);
  var ok=!skill||a._tags.indexOf(skill)>-1;a.hidden=!ok;if(ok)shown++;
  [].forEach.call(a.querySelectorAll(".meta .tags li"),function(li){li.classList.toggle("hit",!!skill&&li.textContent.trim()===skill)});
 });
 count.textContent="Showing "+shown+" of "+arts.length+" projects"+(skill?" with the skill "+skill:"")+", "+(order==="new"?"newest first":"oldest first");
}
sortSel.addEventListener("change",apply);skillSel.addEventListener("change",apply);apply();
})();
</script>
